lesson_title: Two Honest Answers to One Question: FIFO and Weighted Average
hook_text: Same fridge, same juice, same sales — and two different profits. Both correct.
clip_script: Karabo's snack stand buys juice boxes at eight rand. Then the new price list lands and the wholesaler wants ten. Now there are thirty-five boxes in her fridge — some bought at eight, some at ten — and cold juice boxes don't carry receipts. So what is her stock WORTH? Watch both honest answers. She bought forty-five boxes at eight rand and thirty at ten — six hundred and sixty rand for seventy-five boxes — and sold forty at fourteen rand: five hundred and sixty in the tin. Answer one: she always sells the oldest first, so the fridge holds the newest boxes — all thirty ten-rand boxes plus five eight-rand boxes. Fridge: three hundred and forty. Profit: two hundred and forty. Answer two: pool everything — six sixty across seventy-five boxes is eight rand eighty a box. Fridge: three hundred and eight. Profit: two hundred and eight. Two methods, thirty-two rand apart — and look where the thirty-two lives: it is exactly the gap between the two fridge values. Whatever the fridge holds, the profit line released. That is the whole secret of stock valuation: the shelf and the profit share one pot of rands. Which is why the rule is pick one method and KEEP it — because an owner who switches methods in a lean year isn't doing arithmetic anymore. She's telling stories.
visual_style: A glowing fridge with juice boxes stacked in two coloured layers — eight-rand green, ten-rand orange — splitting into two side-by-side timelines; a rand note physically sliding between the fridge and the profit line to show the shared pot.
mood: Playful, crisp, quietly subversive at the close.
pacing: Quick setup, two clean calculation beats, slow reveal of the shared thirty-two rand, pointed ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and value any shelf two ways — then defend your answer.
